notes.written: Written 14 Nov 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: A December Fed rise now looks almost certain

US prices rose faster than expected in October (CPI +0.4% on the month, core +0.3%). Fed Governor Waller said a December rise is likely and a bigger half-point move should be considered; Dallas Fed President Logan wants at least two more rises. Markets now put the chance of a rise on 9 Dec at roughly 85–90%.
US yields jump, the dollar hits an 18-month high

The US 10-year yield rose about 0.3 percentage points this week to around 5.1%, its biggest weekly jump since April 2025, and the 2-year rose even more. The dollar index climbed to about 103.4, its highest since May 2025. The euro slipped to about $1.11 and the pound to about $1.33.

The dollar pushed up to around ¥160, close to levels where Japan has stepped in to buy yen before. Finance Minister Katayama warned against “one-sided and rapid” moves. A Bank of Japan rise in December is widely expected, but the bigger gap with US rates is still pulling the yen down.
Oil slips again as supply recovers

Brent is near $96 and WTI near $89, set for a second weekly fall of about 2% after a 13–16% drop the week before. Gulf exports are recovering and the IEA expects supply to run ahead of demand this quarter. Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz continue, so the risk of a spike remains.
Gold and silver hit one-year lows

Higher yields and a stronger dollar pushed gold down about 5% this week to near $3,890, and silver to about $48.65, both one-year lows. Gold pays no interest, so it suffers when safer US bonds pay more after inflation.
Europe still leaning towards higher rates

Bundesbank President Nagel said another ECB rise is “highly probable”, and chief economist Lane said a December rise would be prudent if nothing changes; markets put it at about 72%. UK growth was strong at 0.7% in Q3. In Australia, consumer and business confidence fell, raising hopes the RBA will now pause.

USD.note: Held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote; two members wanted a rise. After hotter-than-expected October inflation, Governor Waller said a December rise is likely and a half-point move should be considered; markets put a rise on 9 Dec at roughly 85–90%.

EUR.note: Held on 29 Oct (deposit rate 2.50%) after two rises this year. This week Bundesbank President Nagel called another rise “highly probable” and chief economist Lane said a December rise would be prudent if the data hold; markets put it at about 72%.

GBP.note: Raised to 4.00% on 5 Nov, its first rise since 2023, with all nine members voting to raise (Catherine Mann for 4.25%). It expects inflation near 5% by mid-2027 and said policy is “not on a pre-set path”; the next decision is 17 Dec.

JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on 30 Oct in an 8–1 vote (one member wanted a rise). The summary of that meeting, published this week, showed many members want to keep raising rates and some want to move faster; most economists expect a rise to 1.50% in December.

CAD.note: Raised to 2.50% on 28 Oct, its first rise since July 2023, as oil pushes inflation up. Minutes showed members saw uncertainty as no reason to sit still, but with jobs weakening and oil lower, markets see less than a 50% chance of another move in December.

AUD.note: Raised to 4.85% on 3 Nov in a 6–3 vote (three wanted to hold), its fifth rise this year and highest since 2008. Governor Bullock said it is probably good to wait for data after the rise; weak confidence surveys this week support a pause at the 7–8 Dec meeting.

NZD.note: Surprised markets by holding at 2.75% on 28 Oct in a 4–3 vote (three wanted a rise). It still expects to raise later, but rising unemployment (5.7%) weakens the case for a rise on 9 Dec.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed. Chairman Schlegel said on 4 Nov that inflation pressure has picked up (1.5% in October) and the bank “won’t hesitate” to act if needed; the next decision is in December.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged again on 20 Oct (1-year 3.00%); growth support comes mostly from the government. Consumer inflation is only 0.7%, but factory-gate prices are rising fast (5.7%), so a rate cut looks unlikely; the next rate fixing is 20 Nov.

stories.USD: Inflation is still running hot. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, more than the 0.3% expected, and core prices (without food and energy) rose 0.3%. The yearly rate was not published because data for October 2025 was never collected during that year’s government shutdown; petrol alone is up 37.4% on a year. Producer prices rose 0.3% in October, a little below forecast, but are up 6.5% on a year, the most in nearly four years. Jobs remain solid (165,000 added in October, jobless claims 200,000). Fed officials are now openly discussing a bigger rise, and the 10-year yield jumped to around 5.1%. Next: Fed Chair Warsh speaks 16 Nov, retail sales 17 Nov, Fed meeting minutes 18 Nov (UK 19:00), jobless claims and Philly Fed 19 Nov, consumer sentiment 20 Nov, Fed decision 9 Dec.
stories.EUR: Euro-area growth was confirmed at 0.4% in Q3 (1.3% on a year), but it was uneven: Germany grew 0.2%, Italy was flat and France shrank 0.1%, while Ireland’s 5.5% jump flattered the total. Inflation hit 4.0% in October, the highest in three years, driven by energy; without food and energy it was 2.5%. ECB policymakers sounded more hawkish this week: Bundesbank President Nagel said another rise is “highly probable” and chief economist Lane called a December rise prudent if the data hold. Markets put the chance at about 72%. Shoppers are cautious (retail sales −0.7% in September) and unemployment is 6.5%. Next: ZEW investor survey 17 Nov, ECB financial stability review 18 Nov, Lagarde speaks 19 and 20 Nov, consumer confidence 20 Nov.
stories.GBP: The UK economy grew 0.7% in Q3, the strongest since 2024 and 1.9% higher than a year earlier. Services led (+0.9%), helped by AI-related investment, while building work fell 0.7%. September alone grew 0.2%, better than the flat reading expected. The goods trade deficit widened to £22.3bn. The Bank of England raised its rate to 4.00% on 5 November and expects inflation (3.5% in September) to rise towards 5% by mid-2027 because of energy. Governor Bailey said on 9 November that growth has been more resilient than expected and he sees early signs that AI is lifting productivity, but warned of a possible AI bubble in share prices. Next: jobs and pay 17 Nov, October inflation 18 Nov, Bailey speaks 18 Nov, consumer confidence and retail sales 20 Nov, rate decision 17 Dec.
stories.JPY: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on 30 October, but the summary of that meeting, published this week, showed many members want to keep raising rates and some argue for moving faster. Most economists now expect a rise to 1.50% in December. Pay is rising fast (4.6% on a year in September), but households are cutting back hard: spending fell 6.8% on a year in September, far worse than the 3.1% fall expected. Economists expect Q3 growth to come in close to zero, with weak spending and exports offset by strong business investment. The yen is very weak, near ¥160 per dollar, and the finance minister has warned against rapid moves. Next: Q3 GDP 15 Nov (UK 23:50), trade balance 17 Nov (UK 23:50), national inflation 19 Nov (UK 23:30).
stories.CAD: The Canadian dollar had a poor week, falling to around C$1.42–1.43 per US dollar, its weakest since mid-October. Lower oil prices (Canada’s biggest export) and a stronger US dollar both weighed on it, and the gap between Canadian and US two-year yields widened to about 1.5 percentage points. The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.50% on 28 October; its minutes showed members saw uncertainty as no reason to do nothing, but the jobs market is weakening (unemployment 6.7%, private-sector jobs −53,000 in October), so markets see less than a 50% chance of another move in December. Inflation was 3.1% in September. Next: October inflation 16 Nov (UK 13:30), retail sales 20 Nov.
stories.AUD: The RBA raised its rate to 4.85% on 3 November, its fifth rise this year, and Governor Bullock said it is probably good to wait for data after the rise. Surveys this week showed the rises are biting. The Westpac consumer sentiment index fell 2.7% to 78.2, its lowest in four years, and the NAB survey showed business conditions at their weakest since August 2020 (confidence −15). Yet consumers still expect inflation of 5.3% over the next year, well above the RBA’s 2–3% target. Inflation was 4.3% in September and unemployment 4.7%. The Australian dollar fell to about 68 US cents, from 70 a week earlier. Next: Bullock speaks 16 Nov (UK 22:50), wage growth 18 Nov (UK 00:30), October jobs 19 Nov (UK 00:30), RBA meeting 7–8 Dec.
stories.NZD: New Zealand held a general election on 7 November. Early results give Prime Minister Luxon’s National-led coalition 67 of 131 seats, enough for a majority, but about 400,000 special votes are still to be counted and the official result is due on 27 November. The kiwi jumped on the result, its biggest gain in seven months, but gave the move back as the US dollar strengthened, ending near 56 US cents. The economy is weak: unemployment is 5.7% and jobs fell 0.1% in the September quarter. Inflation is 3.7% (Q3) and the RBNZ expects it to rise further because of fuel. Next: inflation expectations 17 Nov (UK 02:00), Governor Breman speaks 18 Nov, trade 18 Nov (UK 21:45), card spending 20 Nov, final election result 27 Nov, RBNZ decision 9 Dec.
stories.CHF: Swiss inflation rose to 1.5% in October, from 1.0% and above the 1.3% expected, the highest since late 2023. Fuel and heating oil drove most of it; core inflation stayed low at 0.5%. SNB Chairman Schlegel said on 4 November that inflation pressure has increased but there are no major knock-on effects so far, and the bank “won’t hesitate” to change policy if price stability is at risk. For now the rate is expected to stay at 0% in December, with markets pricing a possible rise in 2027. The franc weakened this week (about 0.83 per US dollar) as the dollar rallied, though it is a safe haven that tends to gain when global worries rise. Next: no big Swiss releases on the calendar; the next SNB decision is in December.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. Exports jumped 35.2% on a year in October, helped by the AI boom, and imports rose even faster (+41.6%), partly because energy is dearer. The monthly trade surplus shrank to $105.3bn, below the $126.5bn expected, but this year’s surplus has already passed $1 trillion. Prices are split: consumer inflation slowed to 0.7% (0.8% expected), while factory-gate prices rose 5.7%, the most in over four years, as energy and coal costs climbed. Demand at home is soft (retail sales +1.1% in September) as the property slump continues, and lending rates are 3.00%. Next: October retail sales, factory output and unemployment 16 Nov (UK 02:00), lending rates 20 Nov (UK 01:00).

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Brent is near $96 and WTI near $89, heading for a second weekly fall of about 2% after a 13–16% drop the week before. That is about 10% below mid-May levels (Brent about $105–110), but still well above the early-July low near $72. Gulf producers have restored output to about 97% of pre-war levels, the IEA expects supply to exceed demand by about 1.7 million barrels a day this quarter, and the US says it will keep its blockade of Iran rather than resume fighting. The risk has not gone: at least 10 ships were attacked in the first 10 days of November, and Yemen’s Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates. Falling oil was one reason the Canadian dollar weakened this week.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Around $3,890, a one-year low after falling about 5% this week. That is about 17% lower than in mid-May (about $4,700) and roughly a quarter below January’s record. US yields jumped (10-year around 5.1%; after inflation about 2.8%) and the dollar hit an 18-month high as markets priced in a December Fed rise. Central banks are still buying: they added a net 321 tonnes in Q3, according to the World Gold Council.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Around $48.65, a one-year low, down 2.6% on Friday alone. It is roughly 40% lower than in mid-May (about $77–89) and nearly 60% below January’s peak above $115. It faces the same rate headwind as gold plus worries about factory demand as share markets wobble.
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
